sections.b: Hebrews opens with God's final word in the Son (1:1-4) and seven quotations setting the Son above the angels (1:5-14). After a first warning (2:1-4) it reads Psalm 8 of Jesus, who shared our flesh and blood to become 'a merciful and faithful high priest' (2:5-18). Jesus is greater than Moses (3:1-6), and a sermon on Psalm 95 warns the readers not to fall short of God's rest (3:7-4:13). The central section begins: Jesus the high priest who feels for us (4:14-5:10), a sharp warning and an anchor of hope (5:11-6:20), and the long argument from Melchizedek that Jesus is a priest forever by God's oath (7:1-28).

sections.h: How Hebrews reads the Old Testament
sections.b: Hebrews quotes the Greek Old Testament, usually introducing it as God, the Son or the Holy Spirit speaking now ('as the Holy Spirit says', 3:7), and naming a human writer only rarely ('speaking in David', 4:7). It joins texts that share a word (rest in Psalm 95:11 and Genesis 2:2), argues from what Scripture does not say (Melchizedek's missing genealogy, 7:3), and from the time when something was said (David's 'Today' after Joshua, Hebrews 4:7-8; the oath of Psalm 110 after the law, Hebrews 7:28). It sometimes follows the Greek where it differs from the Hebrew: 'angels' for 'God' in Psalm 8, 'a body' in Psalm 40 (Hebrews 10:5).
sections.refs: Hebrews 3:7; Hebrews 4:3-8; Hebrews 7:3; Hebrews 7:28; Psalm 8:5; Psalm 95:7-11

common: Most readers take Hebrews as a sermon to Christians tempted to give up, not as a treatise against Judaism.
Most modern scholars doubt that Paul wrote it; in the early church the Greek East received it as Paul's, while the Latin West long doubted.
uncommon: Adolf von Harnack proposed in 1900 that Priscilla wrote it, which would explain why the author's name was lost.

sections.h: Jesus the high priest in Hebrews
sections.b: Only Hebrews calls Jesus a priest by title, though other books imply his priesthood. It sets out what a high priest must be: taken from among human beings, acting for them before God, offering gifts and sacrifices, gentle with the ignorant, and called by God as Aaron was (5:1-4). Jesus meets each mark: he shared flesh and blood and was tested as we are (2:17-18; 4:15), and God called him with the words of Psalm 2:7 and Psalm 110:4 (5:5-6). But he is a priest of another kind, 'after the pattern of Melchizedek', by God's oath and by an indestructible life, with no successor, who offered himself once for all (7:16-28).

common: Christians agree that Christ is the one high priest whose sacrifice was offered once for all.
uncommon: Churches differ on whether an ordained ministry shares in that priesthood; see the card on Hebrews 7.

sections.b: Hebrews 7 reads Genesis 14:18-20 word by word. Melchizedek's name means 'king of righteousness', his city's name 'peace'. Scripture gives him no father, mother, genealogy, birth or death, so he is 'made like the Son of God' and remains a priest for all time (7:1-3). Abraham gave him a tenth and received his blessing, so Melchizedek is greater than Abraham and than Levi (7:4-10). Psalm 110:4 promises a priest after his pattern, which shows that the Levitical priesthood was not final (7:11-17).
sections.refs: Hebrews 5:6; Hebrews 5:10; Hebrews 6:20; Hebrews 7:1-28; Genesis 14:18-20; Psalm 110:4

uncommon: Some Christians have held that Melchizedek was Christ himself appearing before his birth; Hebrews 7:3 says rather that he was 'made like' the Son.

sections.b: Hebrews 1-2 mentions angels eleven times. God never said to an angel 'You are my son' (1:5); the angels are told to bow down to the Son (1:6); God makes them winds and fire, while the Son's throne lasts forever (1:7-8); they are 'spirits in holy service, sent on duty for the sake of the people who are going to inherit salvation' (1:14). The comparison matters because the law was spoken through angels (2:2), and because the world to come is not placed under angels but under the Son of Psalm 8 (2:5-9).

Hebrews' main title for Jesus is 'Son'. God has spoken 'in a Son' (1:2), the radiance of his glory and the exact stamp of his being (1:3). Psalm 2:7 and 2 Samuel 7:14 are quoted of him (1:5), and Psalm 45:6 addresses him 'O God' (1:8). He is faithful 'as a Son' over God's house (3:6), 'Jesus, the Son of God' is the confession (4:14), and 'even though he was a Son' he learned obedience through suffering (5:8). The argument about priesthood ends with 'a Son made perfect forever' (7:28).
sections.refs: Hebrews 1:2-8; Hebrews 3:6; Hebrews 4:14; Hebrews 5:5-8; Hebrews 7:3; Hebrews 7:28; Psalm 2:7

sections.b: Hebrews reads Psalm 95's 'They will never come into my rest' together with Genesis 2:2, 'on the seventh day God rested'. The wilderness generation failed to enter the land through unbelief. Joshua later brought Israel in, but the psalm, spoken long afterward 'in David', still says 'Today', so the land was not the final rest. God's own rest, open since creation, is still waiting: 'a Sabbath rest is still waiting for God's people' (4:9). Believers are urged to be eager to enter it.

Hebrews uses a rare word, sabbatismos, 'Sabbath-keeping', for the rest that remains for God's people, built on the verb of Exodus 16:30 in Greek, 'the people kept Sabbath'. It links the weekly Sabbath with God's rest after creation (Genesis 2:2) and with the final rest of the world to come. Hebrews uses the Sabbath as a picture of the end, not as a ruling on which day Christians should keep.

Hebrews warns its readers five times: do not drift away (2:1-4); do not harden your hearts (3:7-4:13); those who once received the light and then fall away cannot be brought back to repentance (6:4-8); if we keep on sinning by choice, no sacrifice for sins is left (10:26-31); do not be like Esau (12:14-29). Each warning is joined to assurance: 'about you, beloved, we are persuaded of better things' (6:9). Hebrews 6:4-6 is one of the main texts in the debate over whether believers can fall away; see the card on Hebrews 6.

Hebrews builds its argument mainly on psalms: Psalm 2:7 and 45:6-7 (the Son and his throne), 104:4 and 102:25-27 (angels and creation), 110:1 (the seat at God's right hand), 8:4-6 (the human being crowned with glory), 22:22 (praise among the brothers), 95:7-11 (Today, if you hear his voice) and above all 110:4, 'You are a priest forever, after the pattern of Melchizedek', quoted or echoed throughout 5:6-7:28. It quotes them in Greek and introduces them as God or the Spirit speaking.

sections.b: Hebrews honors Moses with God's own words: 'In all my house he is faithful' (Numbers 12:7). It calls him an 'attendant' (therapōn, the word of Numbers 12:7 in Greek), a trusted servant whose work was 'a witness to things that would be spoken later'. Christ is greater, as a son is over a household and a builder over a house (3:3-6). The comparison continues in 11:23-29, where Moses chooses 'the disgrace of the Messiah'.

sections.h: The wilderness generation as a warning (Hebrews 3)
sections.b: Hebrews 3:7-19 reads Psalm 95 as a warning drawn from the wilderness: Israel saw God's works for forty years, yet quarreled with him and tested him, and the whole generation's corpses fell in the wilderness (Numbers 14:29). The readers are in the same place, rescued and on the way, and could fall short through unbelief. Paul draws the same lesson in 1 Corinthians 10.

Hebrews 7:3 states the direction of a type plainly: Melchizedek 'has been made like the Son of God'. The later figure is the reality; the earlier is shaped to resemble it. Hebrews reads the wilderness generation (3:7-4:11), Joshua's rest (4:8) and the Levitical high priest (5:1-4) the same way, and later uses the words 'copy', 'shadow' and 'pattern' for the tent and its worship (8:5; 10:1).

Hebrews 7:4-10 argues from Abraham's tenth: the one who receives a tithe and gives a blessing is the greater. Levi's descendants took tithes from their own brothers under the law (Numbers 18:21-28), but Melchizedek, from outside their family, took a tithe from Abraham himself, and 'so to speak', Levi paid it too while still in Abraham's body. The argument is about priesthood, not about Christian giving.

sections.h: The high priest behind the veil (Hebrews 4-7)
sections.b: Hebrews reads Jesus' work through the Day of Atonement. He 'made a cleansing for sins' (1:3; compare Leviticus 16:30), makes atonement for the people's sins (2:17), has gone 'right through the heavens' (4:14) and entered 'the inner side of the veil' as forerunner (6:19-20), the phrase of Leviticus 16:2 and 12 in Greek. Unlike Aaron, he needed no offering for himself (5:3; 7:27). Chapters 9-10 develop the comparison fully.
sections.refs: Hebrews 1:3; Hebrews 2:17; Hebrews 4:14; Hebrews 6:19-20; Hebrews 7:27; Leviticus 16:2-30

sections.b: Hebrews uses priestly language for Jesus' death: a cleansing for sins (1:3), tasting death for everyone (2:9), making atonement (hilaskesthai) for the people's sins (2:17), and offering himself once for all (7:27). It also uses the picture of victory: by his death he made powerless the one who wields the might of death and set free those enslaved by fear (2:14-15). The two pictures stand side by side.

Hebrews says Jesus 'has suffered through being tested himself, so he can come to the aid of those who are being tested' (2:18), and that he 'has been tested in all things, in the same way we are, but apart from sin' (4:15). Its fullest picture of his testing is 5:7-8: in the days of his flesh he offered requests and pleading with loud cries and tears, and learned obedience from what he suffered, which most readers connect with Gethsemane.

sections.h: He always lives to plead for them (Hebrews 7:25)
sections.b: Hebrews joins Christ's intercession to his permanent priesthood: because he remains forever, 'he is able to save fully and for all time those who come near to God through him. He lives always, to plead for them' (7:25). Paul says the same of the risen Christ at God's right hand (Romans 8:34), and 1 John 2:1 calls him an Advocate with the Father.

Hebrews names no author. Eusebius reports that some rejected it because the church of Rome disputed that Paul wrote it, and that Gaius of Rome counted only thirteen letters of Paul. The Muratorian fragment does not mention it. The papyrus P46 (about AD 175-225) places it right after Romans among Paul's letters. Jerome wrote that it 'is not considered his, on account of its difference from the others in style and language' (Lives of Illustrious Men 5), and Augustine that 'most say' it is Paul's, 'though some deny this' (City of God 16.22). The African councils of the 390s still put it with Paul's letters: the Council of Carthage of 397 lists, in its Latin, 'thirteen letters of the apostle Paul, one of the same to the Hebrews'. Luther placed Hebrews with James, Jude and Revelation at the end of his New Testament. Every church today holds it as Scripture.

Christ 'takes hold of Abraham's offspring' (2:16). Abraham is the model of patient faith: God swore by himself to bless him, and 'by being patient' he received what was promised (6:13-15). Yet Abraham gave a tenth to Melchizedek and was blessed by him, which makes Melchizedek's priesthood greater than Levi's (7:4-10). Chapter 11 returns to his faith.

Hebrews 6:13-14 quotes the oath God swore after Abraham offered Isaac: 'By myself I swear... I will bless you richly' (Genesis 22:16-17). Hebrews makes that oath the ground of Christian hope: God's promise and God's oath are 'two unchangeable things' (6:18). Hebrews 11:17-19 tells the binding itself.

Hebrews calls God's word 'alive and at work', cutting deeper than a two-edged sword, judging the musings and plans of the heart. In context it is God speaking 'Today' in Psalm 95, the voice the readers must not harden themselves against. The passage ends with a pun: before God's word (logos) we must give our account (logos).

Hebrews 1:3 calls the Son 'the brightness that shines out from God's glory and the exact stamp of his being' (hypostasis), and 1:8 applies Psalm 45:6, 'Your throne, O God', to him. Athanasius used 1:3 against Arius: since light is never without its radiance, there was never a time when the Son was not. The word hypostasis later became the church's term for each 'person' of the Trinity.

sections.h: A change of priesthood, a change of law (Hebrews 7)
sections.b: Hebrews 7:11-19 argues that the Levitical priesthood could not bring perfection, since God promised another priest after the pattern of Melchizedek. 'When the priesthood moves to someone else, a change of law has to come with it' (7:12). The earlier command about priestly descent is 'canceled, because it was weak and did no good (the law did not make anything perfect)'. Christians differ on how far the change reaches; Jewish readers reject the argument.

Hebrews 1:6 calls the Son 'the firstborn' when God leads him into the world and commands the angels to bow down. The title recalls Psalm 89:27, where God makes David's heir 'firstborn, most high over the kings of the earth'. It is a title of rank as well as birth. Hebrews 12:23 speaks of 'the assembly of the firstborn', the church.
